You are part of an optimization system that improves a given text (i.e. the variable). You are the gradient (feedback) engine. Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. The variables may be solutions to problems, prompts to language models, code, or any other text-based variable. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. Only provide strategies, explanations, and methods to change in the variable. DO NOT propose a new version of the variable, that will be the job of the optimizer. Your only job is to send feedback and criticism (compute 'gradients'). For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode...', 'Adding X can fix this error because...', 'Removing X can improve the objective function because...', 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ...', that gets at the downstream objective.
If a variable is already working well (e.g. the objective function is perfect, an evaluation shows the response is accurate), you should not give feedback.

### Glossary of tags that will be sent to you:
# - <LM_SYSTEM_PROMPT>: The system prompt for the language model.
# - <LM_INPUT>: The input to the language model.
# - <LM_OUTPUT>: The output of the language model.
# - <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION>: The objective of the optimization task.
# - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.
# - <ROLE>: The role description of the variable.
payload.instruction: Move the book behind the flower
payload.rubric: Judge requested image editing: yes means all requested changes are complete, no means no requested change has progressed, partial means some progress without complete fulfillment. Unrelated edits are not requested progress. Insufficient evidence stays unresolved.

node.question: Comparing the source and edited images, is there observable progress in the book’s spatial relation to a flower toward the book being behind it?
node.criteria: Pass only when the same book and a relevant flower can be compared and visible evidence shows the book–flower relation itself advancing toward the book being behind the flower—for example, the book becoming occluded by that flower, or a clearly reduced separation specifically along a placement that advances that relation. Fail only when the objects and comparison are clear and affirmative evidence shows no such relational progress, such as the book remaining separate or merely beside the flower, or moving toward/overlapping another object. Proximity, movement alone, changed flower appearance/count, and unrelated scene edits are not progress. Unknown when correspondence or relational change cannot be determined. A completed relation is not a failure for lack of further movement.
node.binding: Compare source and edited images for the book’s spatial relation to a flower, not general book movement or scene similarity. Do not require the edited flower to be the same individual as the source rose if identity is ambiguous; assess whether the visible relation to a flower advances toward the requested behind-flower placement. Do not count adjacency, proximity, or overlap with the open book. Preserve unknown when the relevant comparison is genuinely indeterminate.

node_traces.evidence: The source book and rose are clearly separate. In the edited image, the blue book remains separate from both flowers; it is not occluded by a flower or visibly placed behind one. The scene changes, but the book–flower relation shows no progress toward the requested placement.

The book remains visibly separate from the flowers in the edited image; it is not occluded by either flower or placed closer in a way that advances a behind-flower relation. The scene also changes the book’s appearance, but that does not show the requested spatial progress.
